 Live .  11,561 viewing 11561 viewing Live page Updated 2 minutes ago Passengers face airport delays as US flights resume after nationwide ground stop
 Summary
 US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says a nationwide ground stop has been lifted after an outage halted all flights
 Duffy says the travel chaos will take time to unwind, with many passengers still stranded at airports
 Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin says it was caused by a "telecommunications outage" , and that there's zero evidence this was a cyber-attack 
 Officials have blamed old systems for the outage , saying this could happen again without a "complete overhaul"
 The incident, which started at about 21:00 GMT on Friday and lasted about four hours, was the largest ground stop in the US since the one after 11 September 2001 
 Close form Have you been affected?
 Get in touch Media caption, 'We'll get home one day' - US travellers impacted by nationwide ground stop Live Reporting
 Edited by Tinshui Yeung
 Flight delays expected after US ground stop - what we know published at 06:03 GMT 06:03 GMT 
 Image source, EPA A nationwide ground stop affecting departing flights across the US has been lifted after almost five hours - but passengers can still expect lengthy delays as airports work through the backlog.
 US Transport Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference earlier , where they said the ground stop had been issued due to inconsistent data from outdated equipment. 
 Duffy blamed the outage on old air traffic control systems that have not been updated because of a lack of Congressional funding, and made a plea for $50bn in funding for a new "state-of-the-art system". 
 Mullin reassured the room that there was no evidence that the ground stop was caused by a cyber-attack, or linked to yesterday's Microsoft outage, and that "no one was ever at risk".
 It is only the second time - and the longest - such a stop has been issued since right after the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks.
 Representatives on both sides of politics have called for an investigation into what happened on Friday evening to ensure "it never happens again".

 Photographs paint chaotic picture of nationwide ground stop published at 05:36 GMT 05:36 GMT 
 Image source, EPA Image caption, Travellers line up to rebook tickets at John F Kennedy International Airport
 Image source, EPA Image caption, Travellers rest on the floor amid hours-long delays
 Image source, Reuters Image caption, The departures board at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport shows wall-to-wall delays and cancellations
 Image source, EPA Image caption, Baggage piles up at Washington National Airport as passengers wait for their flights
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Questions remain unanswered after White House press conference, says ex-FBI deputy director published at 05:22 GMT 05:22 GMT 
 Former TSA Administrator John Pistole says he is "not optimistic" about how quickly things are going to get back up and running at airports across the country.
 Pistole, who was also the former FBI deputy director, has told the BBC that there are still a number of questions that remained unanswered after the White House press conference. 
 While he acknowledges "antiquated equipment", he says he still does not know why it happened today - and says this is of major concern ahead of Thanksgiving. 
 The primary question, Pistole says, is "why now". 
 When asked if he agrees with Duffy's assessment that it is a national security issue, Pistole says "absolutely". 
 "If you have a plane go down, that's a bad day for everybody," he says.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Congressional response to stoppage published at 04:45 GMT 04:45 GMT 
 Like so many Americans living through the ground stop and the traffic delays, members of Congress have also expressed their frustration. 
 Some have pointed that frustration in the direction of the Trump administration following Mullin and Duffy's news conference.
 Nevada Senate Democrat Jacky Rosen calls the ground stop "unacceptable" and says there must be an investigation into what happened today to "make sure it never happens again".
 House Democrat Maxwell Frost also calls for an investigation into today's ground stop. 
 Republican Congressman Nick Langworthy, of New York, who chairs the Aviation Safety Caucus, says the disruption shows why Congress cannot put off modernising the FAA's infrastructure. 
 "Modernizing our air traffic control system comes at a significant cost, but the cost of continued failure is far too high," he writes on social media. 
 He also calls for more transparency from the FAA about "what happened, why it happened, and what other vulnerabilities could cause future disruptions". 
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Systems 'thoroughly tested' before ground stop lifted, says FAA published at 04:09 GMT 04:09 GMT 
 The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says it "thoroughly tested" its systems "to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable" before clearing flights to resume.
 "The safety of the flying public is always the FAA’s highest priority," it says on social media. 
 Meanwhile, more airlines have released updates:
 American Airlines says it's focused on "operating as many remaining flights as possible this evening while positioning the airline for the strongest possible recovery in the days ahead"
 JetBlue says it "plans to resume flights on Saturday morning" 
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 United Airlines says some flights resuming published at 03:36 GMT 03:36 GMT 
 We told you earlier that Delta was resuming flights, now we're hearing from United Airlines. 
 The airline says they are resuming "some Friday night flights" in the wake of the FAA lifting its ground stop. 
 "Safety is our highest priority as we take care of our customers and employees," the social media statement goes on to say. 
 United does not make any mention of how future flights, after Friday night, will be impacted.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Delta says flights are resuming published at 03:13 GMT 03:13 GMT 
 Image source, Reuters In the time since the FAA-mandated ground stop has been lifted, we've started to hear from some major American airlines. 
 Among them is Delta Airlines, which has taken to social media to say they were "safely resuming flights". 
 "Thank you for your understanding as we work as quickly as possible to fully restore normal operations," the social media post went on to say. 
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 'Whatever is gonna happen is gonna happen,' says mum stuck at airport published at 02:50 GMT 02:50 GMT 
 Though airspace has now been re-opened, many passengers will remain stranded as airports try to work through a backlog of flights.
 The BBC spoke to Vanessa, who is currently moving interstate with her family from Colorado to Florida.
 Travelling with her husband, two children and five cats, she says that communication from staff at the airport has been really unclear.
 Three donkeys have gone ahead of the family on the trailer, and at this stage, they are likely to beat them to their new home in Florida.
 Vanessa says her kids are a little anxious, but she is trying to remind them that everything is an adventure. 
 "Whatever is gonna happen is gonna happen," she says.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Mood has lifted for some passengers as they board flights published at 02:35 GMT 02:35 GMT 
 Oliver O'Connell 
Reporting from Newark airport 
 There was a big gasp from passengers seated at the gates here in Terminal B at Newark airport in New Jersey, as news broke that the ground stop had been lifted.
 Passengers are now boarding an Alaska Airlines flight to Seattle - gate agents are working quickly to clear the backlog on the concourse as soon as possible.
 Most of the passengers here are supposed to fly across to the West Coast - the mood has lifted but some passengers have been here for almost five hours since their flights were delayed. 
 My 19:23 EST (00:23 GMT) flight is now scheduled for 23:58 EST. Instead of arriving in Los Angeles at a reasonable 22:43 PST, I will now land at 02:54 PST - needless to say, I’m not happy. 
 Image source, Oliver O'Connell 
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 News conference wrapped, here's what we learned published at 02:27 GMT 02:27 GMT 
 Media caption, US ground stop caused by 'incredibly old air traffic control system', Duffy says
 The news conference at the White House has just finished, if you're just joining us, here's what you missed: 
 The ground stop that was impacting millions of Americans has been lifted as of 20:15 EST (01:15 GMT), the US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced
 However Duffy told reporters there was a ripple effect from the closure and problems will persist for days 
 Duffy, along with the Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, put blame for the ground stop on old air traffic control systems that have not been updated because of a lack of Congressional funding
 Mullin reassured the room that there was no evidence that the ground stop was caused by a cyber attack, or linked to yesterday's Microsoft outage, and that "no one was ever at risk"
 Without a "complete overhaul" of the transportation system, Mullin warned something like today's events could happen again 
 Duffy told reporters that while it will take time for the system to become operational again, the systems will be back to capacity before the popular American travel holiday of Thanksgiving
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Duffy says he 'can't anticipate every catastrophic failure' in the network published at 02:19 GMT 02:19 GMT 
 The transport secretary says he "can't anticipate every catastrophic failure" of the network, and that he did not “anticipate an outage like this”.
 “There will be more of them" if the old legacy system is not updated, Duffy says.
 Reporters have questioned how flyers can feel safe returning to the skies, with a system that Duffy says is “too old” remaining in place. 
 Duffy does not specifically address the question, and instead reiterates that he needs the help of Congress to build a new system - it will take time, he says, but now is the moment to act.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Duffy notes similar outages during UN meeting in New York and at Newark published at 02:07 GMT 02:07 GMT 
 Duffy explains that there have been previous issues with networks and outages including when global leaders were flying into New York for the UN earlier this year, as well as issues at New Jersey's Newark airport. 
 "How many more times does this need to happen," he asks.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Things will be 'back up and operational' by Thanksgiving, says Duffy published at 01:59 GMT 01:59 GMT 
 The transport secretary has been asked whether this outage will affect holiday travel.
 Duffy says that it is going to “take us some time to get back to capacity”, but thinks things will be “back up and operational as we come in to the heat of travel during Thanksgiving”. 
 The Thanksgiving travel period, which begins in less than two weeks, is usually one of the busiest times of the year for air travel in the US.
 Duffy has added that larger plane travel is being prioritised over "smaller movements" to try and get things back up and running as quickly as possible.
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Transport secretary Sean Duffy addresses reporters at the White House after all flights in the country were grounded
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Incidents like this could happen again, says Mullin published at 01:56 GMT 01:56 GMT 
 Mullin says a "complete overhaul" of the transportation system is needed and Duffy emphasises that point, saying this won't happen overnight but it's desperately needed. 
 The transport secretary cautions incidents like this one will continue to happen in the future if the transportation system isn't overhauled. 
 If there are any issues, Duffy says they will shut down the system. He says there wasn't a complete blackout in communications during this incident, but it was intermittent, so they decided to enact the ground stop.
 Duffy explains that even though they had some communications, when you have issues and you can't immediately communicate or see planes, "that's a risk that we're unwilling to tolerate".
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 'Zero evidence' of cyber attack, says Mullin published at 01:52 GMT 01:52 GMT 
 A reporter has asked whether the Trump Administration has seen any evidence to indicate a cyber attack. 
 Mullin has said they have assembled teams to investigate this, but at this stage, there is “nothing that indicates” it is an attack and they have “not seen any footprints” of something of that nature.
 “We have seen zero evidence that this is a cyber attack, or an SI attack,” says Mullin. 
 Duffy has followed up by saying the reason for the system outage is clear - it is old, he says, with old routers, and it’s a “national security risk”.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 'It was old legacy equipment that failed', says Duffy published at 01:52 GMT 01:52 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Duffy, who is asking for $50b from Congress to build new air traffic control systems, is explaining how a patchwork fix overwhelmed existing systems. 
 He says that none of the new equipment that they've rolled out recently is to blame.
 "What went down was old. It was old legacy equipment that failed," he says.
 Duffy says that they were able to roll out fixes to "reduce the overloading on our switches that were able to bring the networks back online".
 He says those fixes appeared to help signal that there wasn't an attack, but that it was existing equipment and network failures.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 US has 'incredibly old air traffic control system', Duffy says published at 01:48 GMT 01:48 GMT 
 Duffy has given us a timeline as to how the incident unfolded.
 He says that at 3:36 pm local time, “we experienced instability for our radar and our communications and our centres” across the country. Once inconsistent data from routers started registering, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop.
 “What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy told reporters, explaining that the routers got “overloaded with data”, which led to “inconsistency” in the data received from those routers.
 He went on to say that Congress needs to “give us the resources to build a state-of-the-art air traffic system”, and he needs $50bn to revamp the system.
 Currently the Republican Party controls both chambers of Congress.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Duffy confirms airspace is reopened but fallout will persist for days published at 01:44 GMT 01:44 GMT 
 Transportation secretary Sean Duffy confirms that the airspace has reopened.
 "We've got our centres and our trachons operational right now, and so at 8:15 tonight Eastern time, we've opened up the airspace."
 But flight movement depends on resources, he says. 
 "It's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon."
 Duffy explains the outage will cause a ripple effect, and they are looking at flights this weekend to try to get things back on track, so the problem will persist for a few days.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 The ground stop has been lifted - US media published at 01:38 GMT 01:38 GMT Breaking 
 The ground stop has been lifted, US media are reporting. 
 Some four hours after the halt began, flights will be resuming. 
 US transportation officials are continuing their news briefing from the White House and we expect they will offer more details. 
 We'll bring you the latest as we learn it.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 'No one was ever at risk', Mullin tells White House press briefing published at 01:36 GMT 01:36 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin steps up to the microphone first as the briefing begins. 
 He quashes claims that the outage today has anything to do with the Microsoft outage many experienced yesterday. 
 Mullin says the administration is moving at an unprecedented pace to make sure everyone is safe and helping passengers who are stranded. 
 He adds that the public was never at risk, "no one was ever at risk".
